results.corrected_extracted: The authors note that methadone's long half-life could contribute to the rise in deaths in the first three to four days after leaving, but that deaths rose markedly across the whole first four weeks compared with the treatment period; they suggest this could be explained by loss of tolerance to the toxic effects of heroin, assuming that many people return to use, and probably by use of several legal and illicit substances; they note similar peaks after prison release or hospital discharge, where tolerance is probably diminished, and that deaths from suicide and injury are also more common in that period. The review had no data on tolerance or drug use after leaving.
results.note: Content confirmed; the paragraph opens with the half-life alternative for the first 3-4 days, which the anchor omitted although it qualifies the tolerance explanation.

results.corrected_extracted: Limitations stated by the authors: the same people are compared in and out of treatment, but they leave and re-enter treatment non-randomly, so there could still be a large potential for confounding in crude comparisons, and confounders would need measuring at each exit and re-entry; dropouts are more likely among people at higher risk of death while out of treatment (informative censoring); the amount and direction of the resulting bias in the pooled estimates is hard to assess with the available information; studies were from high-income countries; overdose deaths when substitution medicines were obtained on illicit markets were not captured; a delayed record of leaving could misclassify deaths out of treatment as in treatment (making the estimates conservative); inconsistent overdose definitions and cause-of-death coding could misclassify deaths, which would tend to undercount overdose deaths.
results.note: The source says overdose mortality (not all deaths) was missed for illicitly obtained medicines; added the authors' statement that bias size and direction cannot be assessed (p. 12).

key_findings.correction: The seven atypical accounts: two had injected in places they had never used before (a car-wash bathroom, a candy-store basement); two described unusual injection procedures (one found a vein at the first attempt, unlike her usual difficulty; one accidentally diluted the heroin too much, so that two injections instead of the usual one preceded the overdose); one took a barbiturate mixture (Tuinal) with the heroin, against his usual practice of using no other drug with it; one, who usually injected cocaine with heroin, injected heroin alone for the first time in over 9 months because no cocaine was available; one used with a large group in his own living room at his wedding celebration, and by his account he alone overdosed from the shared supply; in about 10 years of heroin use he had never before taken it in his living room or in so large a group.

Background cited from older sources: about 1% of people dependent on heroin die each year, mostly from an acute reaction to injected heroin (Maurer & Vogel, 1973); many such deaths follow a dose that would not be expected to be fatal for these drug-experienced, and presumably tolerant, people (reviews by Brecher, 1972, and Reed, 1980), sometimes a dose tolerated the day before (Government of Canada, 1973).

reporting_issues.correction: issue: No definition of an atypical circumstance, no classification procedure and no second rater are reported, nor whether the interviewer (H. Berkley, acknowledgment, p. 428) knew the hypothesis. | consequence: The count of 7 of 10 rests on an undescribed classification of open-ended recollections.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible given the hedges and the author's own caveats. Add to 'claimed': the closing summary says overdose 'may be especially likely' in unusual circumstances (p. 429, DISCUSSION, 2nd paragraph), a comparative-risk statement the uncontrolled data cannot test.

Library note for the editor: PDFs/Heroin/Siegel_1982_HeroinOverdoseEnvironmentalCues.pdf is byte-identical (same SHA-256) to this 1984 PDF, so the 1982 Science rat experiment is not on file; the card's description of it is second-hand from p. 429, as the card says.

key_findings.correction: Self-administration cues: the review states that people show more tolerance to alcohol and opiates when they self-administer than when given the same doses on a schedule set by the experimenter, and that animals that self-administer a drug by making a designated response are more tolerant than yoked animals given the same doses at the same times passively; alcohol-experienced people (Mello & Mendelson, 1970) and morphine-experienced rats (MacRae & Siegel, 1997) denied the drug showed more severe withdrawal if they had self-administered it than if they had received it passively.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist (none-applicable) matches the design; domain judgments and overall high agreed.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor agreed for a proponent's model statement. The abstract's 'mediate' is stronger than the body's 'Pavlovian conditioning contributes to tolerance' (p. 297), which the card's 'claimed' could set side by side.

missed: Key finding 5 (corrected): the yoked comparison is stated for 'animals' (p. 298), not rats; the review names no species for it.

outcomes.instruments lists analgesia, which the review's text does not mention (only a reference title mentions hyperalgesia); body temperature, withdrawal signs, caffeine's cardiac effect, alcohol intoxication and reported craving are named.

p. 299, Drug-Onset Cues and Relapse: the clinical claim called well established (small doses precipitate withdrawal and relapse) is supported only by McDonald & Siegel (2004), which pp. 298-299 describe as a rat experiment; p. 296 also calls that paper a review. Strengthens reporting issue 0.
p. 297, 3rd paragraph: the review classes its human examples as opportunistic designs relying on subjects' outside conditioning histories, not explicit cue-drug pairing.

key_findings.correction: Where cohorts reported adjusted estimates (five methadone, one buprenorphine), adjustment to various degrees for demographics, severity of drug use, treatment and comorbidity (Degenhardt 2009 only for age, sex and calendar year) left the all-cause out-to-in ratios unchanged in two methadone cohorts and 15.5% to 35.5% larger in three, and 16.8% larger in the buprenorphine cohort; overdose ratios were unchanged in three methadone cohorts and 25.8% and 28.6% larger in two, Evans 2015 and Nosyk 2015, whose overdose ratios combine maintenance with detoxification or include never-treated participants (Table 4 footnote). [page: pp. 4, 9]

The authors note that methadone's long half-life could contribute to deaths in the first three to four days after leaving, but suggest that the excess across the first four weeks could be explained by loss of tolerance to the toxic effects of heroin, assuming many people return to use, and probably by use of several substances; they note similar peaks after prison release and hospital discharge and more deaths from suicide and injury in that period. No data on tolerance or drug use after leaving were available to the review.

Limitations stated by the authors: people leave and re-enter treatment non-randomly, so confounding may be large; people lost to follow-up may be at higher risk (informative censoring); the amount and direction of the resulting bias in the pooled estimates is hard to assess; overdose deaths when substitution medicines were obtained illicitly were not captured; delayed records of leaving could misclassify deaths; overdose definitions and coding varied; all studies came from high-income countries.

reporting_issues.correction: issue: Three of the unadjusted rate ratios in Table 4 differ from the crude ratios implied by Figs 2-3: Degenhardt 2009, all causes, 1.91 (Fig 2: 14.3/5.8 = 2.5); Nosyk 2015, all causes, 3.04 (130.2/22.4 = 5.8); Buster 2002, overdose, 0.87 (Fig 3: 2.4/2.2 = 1.1). The Table 4 footnote explains only the overdose ratios of Evans 2015 (maintenance combined with detoxification) and Nosyk 2015 (never-treated participants included), neither of which is in Fig 3; the three differences are not explained. | consequence: The percentage changes after adjustment refer to the primary studies' own models, which for some cohorts used other person-time than the pooled data.

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low agreed (items 2 and 7). Item 11 'yes' is generous: for non-randomized studies AMSTAR 2 asks for adjusted estimates or a stated justification for pooling raw data, and crude rates were pooled without one; 'no' would not change the overall.

interpretation_gap.note: Domain: abstract conclusions and summary box. Substantial, not minor: the abstract presents methadone induction as particularly risky (ratio 0.94 to 4.10; one-cohort trend) and says overdose evolved similarly (4.2 vs 3.4); the box is counterfactual; between-drug significance has no test. The card's own 'claimed' text documents this.

missed: Replication timeline: Degenhardt 2009 is called the largest included methadone cohort (31,846 participants), but Evans 2015 has more participants (32,322, Table 2); Degenhardt is largest by person-years (217,273 of 514,214 in Fig 2, 42%).

where_it_stands says the direction, including a high-risk period after leaving, is the same in all 16 methadone cohorts; the post-leaving peak was measured only in the five cohorts with interval data (all five agree, Fig 4).

p. 7, Discussion: the authors' proposed explanations for early-treatment risk (methadone accumulating beyond tolerance given its 22-hour mean half-life; tolerance not fully protecting against respiratory depression; psychological factors; other respiratory depressants or cocaine) are hypotheses without data in the review.

Key finding 4 context: Buster 2002 crude overdose rates are nearly equal in and out of treatment (2.2 vs 2.4, Fig 3) and its own unadjusted overdose ratio is 0.87 (Table 4), so 'higher out of treatment in every overdose cohort' should not be claimed without that qualifier.

key_findings.correction: Documented deaths during the withdrawal process are all in jail settings and date back to the late 1990s: in 1998 a woman in custody in the UK went into heroin withdrawal with persistent vomiting, sudden weight loss and dehydration; her death was attributed to hypoxic brain damage caused by a cardiac arrest, and a failure of duty of care was argued successfully before the European Court of Human Rights.

Substitution treatment for people dependent on opioids entering custody is described as associated with lower mortality and better outcomes after release than enforced withdrawal; one study is cited as reporting that continued maintenance treatment was associated with a 93% reduction in the risk of death in custody over a 10-year period.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist fits an editorial (house practice); domain judgments and overall high agreed; Larney co-authors refs 9 and 10, Farrell ref. 9.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor agreed: the central claim (such deaths occur) rests on documented cases; the unsupported parts (rising number, every case preventable) are recorded in 'claimed' and reporting issue 2.

missed: replication.timeline, 1998 entry: 'died of hypoxic brain damage after cardiac arrest' should say the cause of death was attributed to it, as in corrected key finding 3.

p. 199, 2nd paragraph: the editorial answers a public claim, attributed to a prominent medical practitioner, that no one dies of opiate withdrawal (ref. 2, a 2009 magazine column); useful context for the question in people's words.
p. 199, 6th paragraph: the authors say the reported jail deaths clearly involved suboptimal withdrawal management; this judgment rests on press and legal reports, not records the authors reviewed.
